text_fidelity_a: MONOPOLY: Fortnite Edition Board Game Inspired by Fortnite Video Game Ages 13 & Up This version of Monopoly does not use money! Genius idea for very little children! Even my 4-year-old loved playing. It can be very quick (which was perfect!). I was out before I ever passed Go, haha. Instead of money, this game uses green circles called HP. You gradually lose them all to the “bank” in the middle, but you can get more by passing Go or by landing on a plus-one space or by drawing a particular card. When you land on an available property, it’s yours for free. If you land on an owned property, you have to pay a green HP. Simple. This game is easy to understand, super fun, and quick for the short attention spans of young Fortnite players. Instead of everyone starting on Go, we all started on a homemade Battle Bus, jumping off and landing on whatever space you want. So we all started the game in different areas of the board and all started with a property. That helped the game go faster and was just plain fun to copy Fortnite. My kids have already played this 5 times in 2 days. Great buy! I rate this board game A+.

text_fidelity_a:
Castle Panic 2nd Edition | Family Board Game | Board Game for Adults and Family | Cooperative Board Game | Ages 8+ | for 1 to 6 Players | Average Playtime 45 Minutes | Made by Fireside Games I purchased this game with the intention of playing with my 5 year old daughter, wife, and possibly my 4 year old son. This has proven to be a great game. I don't think most avid gamers would find it as fun, simply because the design is you play against random board mechanics. Some real bad draws and no matter how good you are, you just can't beat it. Other times, it's skill and other times it's just luck of the draw.

That said, this game is EXCELLENT! There's no heavy competition (unless you use some of the modified rules). Basically, everyone WINS or everyone LOSES. That means my daughter's not nagging her brother, etc, etc. It's a great family game for this reason where it is cooperative. The theme is also the fun part, while you're playing, you will have nail biting times, and easier times, etc. We just purchased it and have played it over 5 times in the last week. My nephews have come over and played multiple times too. It's also great because it can host up to 6 players, which is excellent!

The only downfall I've seen is this. Avid gamers might not like it as it's light in strategy, meaning it's easy to play (almost self guided at times). Also, this game can be harder to play at certain player numbers. For example: 2 players each player has 6 cards, and that's 12 total to look at. With 5 players, there's 5 x 5 hands meaning 25 cards making the odds alot better. Basically 2 and 3 player games can be rough. Lower player games aren't unwinnable, it's just higher difficulty (which again is mostly random). Out of 5 stars I definitely rate this a 4. i would give it a 5 if it wasn't so random (meaning hopeless on some games). By the way, out of 5 games played, we've won 4...so it's not 'that' hopless really...great game!!!
text_fidelity_b: Castle Panic 2nd Edition | Family Board Game | Board Game for Adults and Family | Cooperative Board Game | Ages 8+ | for 1 to 6 Players | Average Playtime 45 Minutes | Made by Fireside Games

Hasbro Gaming Yippie Yippie Yeti Game We just aren't overly fond of this game. It ended up being super frustrating for us.

When you first open the game, you have to put the game board together. This takes a bit of time, but it's not too bad. It looks nice enough, and I like that the game board is thick and sturdy. My boys love the whole idea of the game, and I don't think we've ever played a game where the board stood up. That was really cool! Our biggest issue is how difficult it is to keep the climbers in place. They're constantly falling when they shouldn't be. My children are 3, 5, and 8, so that may have a great deal to do with it. Keeping those climbers hanging where they should proved impossible for us, though. It's also a little frustrating that each player has to move around to play. The game board only faces one way, and you can't move it without making the climbers fall off(even more). That means when 4 people are playing, you can't just sit in a spot and enjoy the game. You have to move around, depending on whose turn it is. That might not be a big deal for many, but it frustrated my little guys.

Overall, we really like the whole idea of the game, and the fact that the game board stands up, but it ended up being incredibly frustrating for everyone.
text_fidelity_b: Hasbro Gaming Yippie Yippie Yeti Game

text_fidelity_a:
The Wolves Board Game | Wolf Themed Survival Strategy Game | Highly Interactive Family Game for Kids and Adults | Ages 14+ | 2-5 Players | Avg. Playtime 75 Minutes | Made by Pandasaurus Games The Wolves is a quick game that looks easy to play, but it sure is not that.

The basic mechanic of the game is to manipulate your terrain tiles to perform actions, each of which can influence how fast the game accelerates, and how you manage to score points. Everything is controlled by these terrain tiles, and so you might choose a move actions specifically so that you can flip a tile that will allow you to use a Howl action. Or you may be lucky enough to flip three matches to Dominate an opponent's wolf, but that would require a lot of luck...or is it skill?

I would compare this game to 5 Tribes. None of the mechanics are similar in any way, but if you've played 5 Tribes, you might know that on your turn, you can likely identify ten different moves you could do, but it's mathematically impossible to always choose the correct action. In this game, you have a similar conundrum. What is the best move? Is it to howl at a wolf to put an extra marker on the board, or build a den that helps me establish area majority? There are turns where you legitimately have to decide between 5 different, equally powerful moves you can make, and then live with those consequences.

I do have one problem with the game, though, and that is that there are a lot of little rules to remember. Two pieces per space, you cannot be moved if you share a spot with a den, you have to re-move if someone "pushes" your pack wolves with an alpha, and alphas are the only ones who can howl. Dens can be upgraded to lairs if your den is next to water, but some spaces have rivers on them that look like water sources, but they aren't. Also, alphas have to be on the space to build a den, but can be adjacent to upgrade it. You get a reference card for some of this, and some is on the board, but it can be tricky to remember all of the specific placement rules for each different action.

This game is a lot thinkier than you might expect, and so it won't be for everyone. Everyone will want to play it though - the production quality of the game, from the art to the unique wolf meeples, is really quite excellent, and the game is rife with possibilities for expansions. The box insert is well-designed, and the maps are modular, which is great for replayability. Overall, our heavy gaming family liked our two plays of the game, and will come back to it often, because not too many games of this depth can be played this quickly.
text_fidelity_b: The Wolves Board Game | Wolf Themed Survival Strategy Game | Highly Interactive Family Game for Kids and Adults | Ages 14+ | 2-5 Players | Avg. Playtime 75 Minutes | Made by Pandasaurus Games

text_fidelity_a: Monterey LG8510 Lady Bug Lure, Pack of 3 I buy these lures each year ever since I learned that ladybugs like to cluster in small hollow space in houses. One year I had 1 exterior wall with over 1000 ladybugs crawling on it in the sunshine, a day later they were all gone and over the following weeks they started falling out of the cracks inside my house. Every morning as soon as the sun rose I would start finding them everywhere. I checked the internet and found the Ladybuglady who told me that ladybugs cluster in the late fall to stay warm through the winter. If they find a space like a house and a way in they will literally take over the sun side wall of the house. The way to avoid this was to build ladybug houses (similar to bird house but with smaller holes) and place them in your garden and orchards where the Ladybugs will benefit your plants (they eat aphids) and get these lures to draw them to the houses. Well for 2 years it has worked like a charm. No ladybugs in my houses and the trees in my orchard are doing very well.

My kiddo was at a play-date recently, and the friend had a plastic set that the kids really enjoyed playing with. I saw these for review and thought they’d be a great addition to our play area at home. One thing I noticed right from the start is that they sound like baby rattles—you can really hear the magnets moving around inside as you move them. I didn’t notice this type of noise with the plastic ones at the play-date, so just something to keep in mind.

The wood is very smooth and each piece is lightweight. They appear to be durable as I don’t notice any bend if I put pressure on one of the pieces, but they also seem thin at the same time. I’m a little concerned that if someone steps on these by mistake, one of them could crack in half and expose little magnets everywhere. Up until this point, I’ve avoided a lot of toys with magnets, so I’m just going to have to be selective about when we play with these so I can really supervise how they’re being used.

Like magnets naturally do, sometimes the sides won’t link correctly if the positive and negative sides are connected right, so this is a normal learning curve for kids. Otherwise, they stand together very well and there’s plenty of pieces and shapes to build some neat things. These are very nice overall, and if you prefer wooden toys, these are a very good option.

text_fidelity_a:
Advantus 12 Inch Desktop World Globe with Blue Oceans (30502),13 W x 12 D x 15 H in Does a perfect globe exist? Probably it does, but I couldn’t afford it. I’m happy with this one although it isn’t perfect.
The good stuff: it came in a super sturdy box that held the globe stable during transport. (The manufacturer ships it, not Amazon.) The stand seems strong and sturdy, and of course I’m grateful for the 720° rotation. The colors are attractive. I even like the raised texture where there are mountain ranges. I’m glad that the United States is divided into states. Finally, although I’m not 100% educated on geography, I can say this globe is up-to-date enough for my purposes; for example, Sudan is divided into Sudan and South Sudan.
The less-good stuff: I’m surprised to see that Canada’s provinces are named, but not outlined! Unless the lines are just so fine that I can’t see them, you have to guess their boundaries. Some cities are identified in the US states, but I was really surprised to see that state capitals are not identified! I suppose some state capitals are named, but Austin Texas (where we live), Tallahassee Florida, and other states I’m familiar with have various cities but not their capitals identified! I also think that city placement is close, but not 100% accurate. Nevertheless, this globe will get a lot of use in homeschooling, and will serve our purposes. I would buy the same globe again if I needed to for some reason.
text_fidelity_b: Advantus 12 Inch Desktop World Globe with Blue Oceans (30502),13 W x 12 D x 15 H in

text_fidelity_a:
Kanagawa Game Kanagawa is a board game about making the most cohesive panorama painting.

The first thing you'll notice about Kanagawa is that it has tremendous components. The little paintbrush bits are unique and well-made, and the way that the cards fit together is really cool. The art and graphic design make it easy for players to figure out how to play, and even the board is well-designed.

Unfortunately, gameplay is pretty basic. Each turn, new cards will be put on the board, either face up or face down depending on the positioning. Players can then either take some of the cards, or allow more to come out, opening up the opportunity to their opponents to take the "best" cards. You then place these cards in panorama fashion on your piece of art, or you can use them as "skill" cards to allow you to paint more interesting paintings on later turns. There are bonus cards, and opportunities to gather more items, but that's really about it.

Aside from the excellent artwork, the only other good thing about this game is that you can explain the rules in only a few minutes. Decisions that you make along the way really are not all that important along the way. You can collect a lot of abilities along the way that you never get the opportunity to use, or you can find that you'd rather not use them because there are better moves for you. Overall, this game was pretty fast, easy to learn, but felt like your decisions were pretty arbitrary, and didn't matter in the end.
text_fidelity_b: Kanagawa Game

text_fidelity_a:
Nerf N-Strike Elite Stryfe Blaster (Colors May Vary) I bought 2 of these blasters for my daughter and I. We have Nerf battles in the house and She wanted a semi auto (to back up her Recon and Maverick) and I need a backup for the Hail Fire. This is a clip system balster with a fly wheel launcher (need 4 AA batteries). All in all I'm pretty pleased.
Good: This blaster does a lot of things well. It is a semi-auto (requires 4 AA batteries), but does not feel heavy or unbalanced. Easy to shoot 1 handed and can be double wielded. Clip system is nice as we have a lot of extra clips so reloads are fast. The clip release button has a good positive feel and has not accidentally relesed a clip yet. The blaster has a top and bottom tactical rail and will accecpt a stock and barrel extention (although why you would want to do this is questionable as it takes away the intent of this compact blaster). Handgrip is comfortable but may be to small for XL hands. Accel. button has a good feel to it. There are 2 place for sling attachment and both spots are logical! Battery door is a sigle screw affair. Accuracy is better than expected (I can hit a human size target 5 out of 6 times at a 30 foot range). Battery life has been good and Rechargables offer no problems.
Bad: This blaster has more safety switches than a modern Table Saw! There is the jam door switch, the clip sensor switch, dart sensor switch, voltage switch (regulator), accel trigger switch, and probably others that I haven't come across yet. The main trouble maker is the dart sensor switch. It works great until the last dart in the clip. Sometimes the dart pressure is not enough to press the switch arm so the blaster won't fire the last dart (VERY ANNOYING!) The easiest NONE WARRENTY VOIDING fix is to open the jam door, take a thin (about 1/8" wide) piece of duct tape (about 2 inches long) and tape the switch to the top of the reciever. I taped it up and around the body and out the top of the jam door. After aprox 100 shots the tape is still holding and I have yet to have a dart left in the clip. The gun is also prone to jamming if you pull the trigger slowly. When firing off a dart you need to make sure to pull the trigger crisply. This only seems to be a problem on the first shot (probably because I usually empty the clip after that first shot). Another problem I've seen is the dislike this blaster has for non-elite darts. If your first dart in the clip is a streamline version you can almost be assured a jam (funny that it only happens if the non-elite is in the first position on the clip- load it farther down and it fires like any other dart). Honestly if your gonna use this for any formal matches stick to the Elite darts. Range is about 35 to 40 feet- hard to get any further.
Final thoughts: This is truely a fun blaster. It does have a few kinks to it, but nothing that a little duct tape can't fix. It is compact enough to carry as a secondary blaster, but combined with additional clip options (I'm thinking an 18 with a couple six back-ups) this could be a close quarters primary blaster. At the current $20 this is really a no brainer.
text_fidelity_b: Nerf N-Strike Elite Stryfe Blaster (Colors May Vary)

text_fidelity_a:
Scrabble Turbo Slam My feelings about this product are mixed -- We've long been fans of Scrabble, and thought we'd shake things up a bit by trying a different variation of the game. The Electronic Turbo Slam device, first required (3)- AAA batteries (not included). The device, when slammed has pretty loud sound effects/music, which I found annoying after a short while. I also thought there was too much commotion for me with everyone trying to slap down cards to change the letters, and I wasn't crazy about making just (4) letter words. As an adult, baby boomer, I much prefer the standard game of Scrabble -- quiet, relaxed and educational, and with more word potential.

I can see that this would be a great game for parents to play with young children to help them get interested in learning new words -- I would use it as an educational tool, instead of having them feel pressured to make words at record speed.

On the other hand, the speed and noise factor, would probably appeal to lots of teens. Overall, the game is relatively inexpensive, and worth a try for families who enjoy word faster paced, action filled games.
text_fidelity_b: Scrabble Turbo Slam

Magformers Hi-Tech LED Lighted Set (55-pieces) I was sort of surprised at how much this light set cost. I probably wouldn't have bought it due to that fact. However, if you have the bucks I think your kids will be very pleased with it. I have two kids ages 10 and almost 12. I got the Magformer Light set in the mail yesterday afternoon and they have been playing almost non-stop with it. It's not unusual for my kids to play with something for a few hours then never touch it again. However, this is the second day and they are still going strong with this set.

It does stimulate the imagination and the pieces are pretty cool imho. They adhere fairly strongly to each other by using internal magnets. They come in various shapes and cool colors and have a battery pack that can be attached to cause the entire creation to light up in multiple colors. The husband and I both had to wear helmets that emitted wonderful colors.....sorry no pics (thank gawd). A USB cable comes with the set to be used to recharge the battery pack.

The kids have multiple Zhu Zhu pets and have been having a blast with those silly things and light set at the same time by building lighted carry cages, homes, space ships and everything else you can think of and cram a zhu-zhu pet inside of. I like this light set a lot, it gives the kids something different and obviously very fun to do, and it has kept their attention now for 2 days straight. I asked them how much they liked it and they both hollered, "We LOVE it!".

LeapFrog LeapTV Dance and Learn Educational, Active Video Game I received this game through the Amazon Vine Program, although the usual green writing may not be written above.

This game is pretty good if your kid is young enough to get excited over "dancing" to burn off energy. There are a bunch of mini games to do alone or with friends that require body movement to excel at.

The deal with the lighting is this, and it applies to all the camera based games: if you have low light, the camera may not register your hand is moving in front of something that is dark, and therefore will not pick up on the movement. So, for example, when I am using ambient light and the living room is not bright, my red couch looks almost black on the screen, so if you have to touch something that is in that area, it won't pick up on it. Similarly, if you turn on the lights, those items will be picked up automatically. Add light or put a white sheet on the couch, in that case.
text_fidelity_b: LeapFrog LeapTV Dance and Learn Educational, Active Video Game

hand2mind Rekenrek Pop-Up Learning Activity Center, Math Games for Kids, Abacus for Kids Math, Math Manipulatives, Montessori Materials for Preschool, Kindergarten Homeschool Supplies I love these kits! They are a wonderful and painfree way to get a bit of math learning into our days. We have three of them now and my children love them. It's basically games. I love that everything I need is right here in this box. I have to do no prep whatsoever, which is great. It's perfect for those rough, stress filled days.

Within this kit, you get a storage box that doubles as an easel. The 10 activities are attached to the box by a spirally bound book. Each of the activities are on both sides of the easel, so that children can sit on each side of it and still be able to see. It also comes with 2 mini Rekenreks, 4 double sided dry erase boards, 4 dry erase markers, 20 number cards, 2 spinners, and a guide.

This particular kit taught me the difference between a Rekenrek and an abacus. Sadly, I'd never even heard of a Rekenrek beforehand. Apparently, it's much better for younger children to learn number problems with, since it changes colors every 5 beads, instead of 10. Plus, it's usually just 20 beads total, like the ones in this kit, and great for little hands.

If your child could use extra practice with adding and subtrating, or just working with numbers 1-20, this is a nice kit to try.
text_fidelity_b: hand2mind Rekenrek Pop-Up Learning Activity Center, Math Games for Kids, Abacus for Kids Math, Math Manipulatives, Montessori Materials for Preschool, Kindergarten Homeschool Supplies

PLANET BAKE Vegan Donut Making Kit - Plant-Based, Gluten Free Donut Kit with Pre-Measured Ingredients & Silicone Donut Molds - Complete Kids Baking Set for Ages 4-12 (Vanilla) I also tried the chocolate version of this donut kit and was quite disappointed in the taste of the donuts. This vanilla option is much better. In anticipation of less than ideal taste I added some good quality vanilla extract which also helped boost the flavor.

Still, the issues I had with the chocolate version are also present in this version. The box it comes in is cheap and flimsy, and dented up quite a bit in transit. It makes for a poor presentation should this be a gift item. On the plus side, the sprinkle packet stayed closed in the vanilla kit box (it broke open in the chocolate kit box and there were sprinkles everywhere). The frosting packet is inside the main pouch with loose flour, so it's a messy proposition to get the frosting packet out -- flour spills easily. Lastly, the silicone molds are quite flimsy. Putting them into something supportive, such as a muffin tin, is highly recommended prior to filling and baking.

The vanilla donuts have a much better flavor than the chocolate, especially when additional vanilla extract is added. The assembly process is simple and, while kids will need supervision (especially when dealing with the silicone molds) it's a fun activity.

Taking all the pros and cons into consideration puts my score at 3.5 stars. It's a great idea, but some of the kinks need to be ironed out to make it a kit that is worth the price charged.
text_fidelity_b: PLANET BAKE Vegan Donut Making Kit - Plant-Based, Gluten Free Donut Kit with Pre-Measured Ingredients & Silicone Donut Molds - Complete Kids Baking Set for Ages 4-12 (Vanilla)

text_fidelity_a:
Little Tikes Dozer Racer 2-in-1 Rc Vehicle for Kids UPDATE 10/10/18: The kids just love this RC car now that it works fine. It's frequently used by a 5-year-old boy and an 8-year-old girl, and it's holding up well to this heavy use. It is easy enough for the 5-year-old to work the controls, but entertaining enough for the 8-year-old to play with it with him. It doesn't run through the batteries as fast as I thought it would either.

UPDATE 9/18/18: I received the replacement toy, and it works perfectly. The toy is so fun and a good price for what you get. I wouldn't hesitate to buy one as a present in the future.

UPDATE 9/10/18: Yesterday (Sunday), I sent an e-mail to customer support about the malfunction. I received a reply early this morning. It was a real person who communicated clearly and actually addressed my problem. They're sending a replacement that has been tested to make sure it works fine. They're also sending a pre-paid return label for the return of the malfunctioning toy so their engineers can look at the unit. I'm super impressed.

ORIGINAL REVIEW (3 stars): This is generally such a fun, nice toy that I almost gave it 4 stars even though I would have returned this toy if I'd actually bought it. The remote is fairly simple: hold down the left button to turn left, hold down the right button to go right, hold both down to go forward. These button work great. But one of the transform buttons had a glitch from the beginning. The vehicle starts out as a race car when you turn it (and the remote) on. When you hit the bulldozer button, that transforms the race car into a bulldozer just fine every time. However, if the user likes to frequently switch back and forth between the two, the race car transform button will malfunction once out of every two or three times you hit it. When it malfunctions, instead of transforming into a race car, the bulldozer goes straight backward until it runs into something. Since there is no stop button, there is no way to stop the crash. You're no longer in control. At this point, the remote control commands do nothing, and you have to lift the vehicle to access the on/off switch to turn it off and on before it will work again. So far, it hasn't damaged the RC vehicle or anything else. However, this malfunction is a bother at the very least and will damage something eventually.

It's a cute toy that the kids really enjoy...as long as they don't transform often and crash every few minutes. The vehicle measures 10.5" long, 5.25" tall, and 7" wide. It requires 6 AA batteries--4 for the vehicle and 2 for the remote control. (Yes, we put brand new batteries in and tried another batch to see if the batteries were behind the problem. No improvement.) The toy is strong enough to push the box that it came in when in the bulldozer mode, and it can handle travel in a yard (at least when we tested it on a freshly mowed lawn). Intended for ages 3+. It certainly works well for the 5 year old boy who mainly plays with it. Made in China.
text_fidelity_b: Little Tikes Dozer Racer 2-in-1 Rc Vehicle for Kids

Magic The Gathering: Arena of the Planeswalkers Game This is a great value for what you're paying. Essentially, this game is based on another very good game called Heroscape. You'll build an arena out of the little pieces in this box, create an army, and do battle with one of the prepainted Planeswalker minis.

I picked this game up as a former MtG player. I was hugely involved in the game from Ice Age through Darksteel. I invested thousands of dollars in the game until it finally became apparent that I couldn't afford to continue to be competitive in the game. What I love about this is that there is a little of what I like about MtG - the deckbuilding, the spellcasting and the strategy - but not so much of what I don't like - the cost.

The game itself is solid if not spectacular. It accomodates up to 5 relatively seamlessly, and it's easy to set up the game as a 2 vs. 2 if you like the team approach, or to just make it a free-for-all. The biggest problem to me with the game, enough to lower it two full stars, is that the game feels like it is missing some essential element that will be added through expansions. It's difficult to identify exactly what it is, but I can't shake the feeling that they took something essential out and going to release it as a big box expansion in the next few months.

As it is, it's a solid game that feels unfinished. I'll eagerly look forward to the (I"m assuming) forthcoming expansion.
text_fidelity_b: Magic The Gathering: Arena of the Planeswalkers Game

We lost a couple on christmas when we opened the gift.. and then a few more since. We have less than half left now (which I think is an accomplishment since we’ve had it almost a year!).

My toddler and her friends have enjoyed playing with it, but they have 1) been hurt by his hard material build (just minor boo boo, but still) 2) tried to eat the teeny pellet foods (cause, why not?) and 3) shoved other objects in its mouth that they weren’t supposed to. The design concept isn’t bad, but I do wish it was slightly bigger, with slightly bigger treats, a slightly longer leash, slightly more “squeezable”... you catch my drift. And with all that in mind, I probably would have gone with a different puppers.
